Re-implementation of grid-poly in a somewhat more traditional way:

1. `d.vary` lets x & y be dragged freely.
2. `spec.during` keeps the dragged point inside the grid.
3. `spec.onDrop` rounds the point to the nearest grid point on drop.
4. `spec.withSnapRadius` works on top of all of this – which is kinda cool because we never enumerate the drop locations!

But note that we don't stop points from colliding, which grid-poly does.

Solve for *x* by dragging, after [Graspable Math](<https://graspablemath.com>). Drag a term along its side to reorder it, or across the **=** to subtract it from both sides. Drop a term on a like term to add them, a number on a number to multiply them, a factor on a parenthesized sum to multiply it out (grab a sum by its parentheses), a power on a power of the same base to add exponents, or a factor on its match across a fraction bar to cancel.

Drop an exponent on its base to work it out or write it as a product, drag it across the **=** to take a root, or drag it out of a log to the front. Drag the base of a power across to take a log, the base of a log across to exponentiate, or drop a log's base on its argument to work it out.

notes.markdown: Proof by dragging, after [Actema](<https://www.actema.xyz/>) and Chaudhuri's *subformula linking*. Each row is a sequent: hypotheses ⊢ goal. **Drag a hypothesis or the goal onto a matching subformula of opposite polarity** (targets light up blue) to link them: the goal (or hypothesis) rewrites, and any new obligations emerge in place. The link happens as soon as you reach the target, and you come away holding what it rewrote, so you can keep going: drag *p* over *p → q* and you're now dragging *q*; if the link finishes the sequent, that's done too. Click a highlighted root connective to split a conjunction, introduce an implication, or case on a disjunction. The proof is done when no sequents remain.

Drag AST boxes to reorder them or move them into/out of groups; drag letters and **\*** from the palette onto the tree; drag a **\*** badge to another box to move the star, or to the trash to unwrap. The NFA below is re-derived from the tree on every drag.

A Gantt chart with dependencies. Start times are never stored: each task starts when its prerequisites are done, plus an optional lag (shown as a dotted lead-in). Drag a bar to change its lag; everything downstream moves with it. Drag the right edge to change duration. Drop a bar onto another task to make that task a prerequisite (targets that would create a cycle are dimmed). Drag the grip on the left to move between resource lanes. Click an arrow to remove it. The critical path is highlighted in red and updates live; grey numbers show slack.

A layout editor for a CSS-like flex/grid model. The layout engine is the render function, so every edit reflows the whole tree. Drag a colored leaf or a dashed box to move it between containers or reorder it. Drag a leaf's corner to resize it. Each box has handles: the circled arrow on its edge switches direction (right edge = row, bottom = column, corner = grid); the small tick in the first gap adjusts the gap; the corner bracket adjusts padding; grids have a dot after the first row to change the column count. Alongside, the same layout as HTML and CSS, rendered by the browser.

A ZX-calculus string diagram editor where every drag is a rewrite rule. **Drag spiders** past each other (interchange), **drop** one on an adjacent same-colored spider (fusion; a bare phase-0 spider drops on any neighbor: identity), **Alt-drag** out of a spider (unfusion), **drag a phase label** onto a same-colored neighbor, **drag a wire's bead** sideways (and through a twin wire: Hopf), and **drag a cup past its cap** (snake).
Two CNOTs in a row cancel. Fuse the Zs, fuse the Xs, then grab the bead on one of the twin wires and pull it across the other wire (Hopf: they cancel). Finally drop each bare spider on a neighbor.

λ-terms as nested boxes. **β-reduce** by dragging an argument onto the binder (the *x* in *λx.*) of the λ it's applied to: as you go, each *x* in the body turns into a copy of the argument, and when you drop, the λ dissolves. Drag a subterm **rightward out** of an enclosing box to abstract over it (the reverse).

A pivot table. Drag field chips between *Rows*, *Columns*, *Values*, and the unused *Fields* pool, or reorder them within a zone. The table re-pivots live as a preview. Cells are keyed by their group (which dimension values they aggregate), so a cell keeps its identity — and glides to its new spot — when a dimension moves between Rows and Columns.

Six views of one Catalan object, all drawn from a single state. Drag a **diagonal** to flip it, drag a **tree node** up to rotate it, slide a **hump** of the Dyck path diagonally (a rotation moves a whole excursion past a down-step – the Tamari move, not a single peak flip) or its **arc** in the pairing, or slide a **parenthesis**. Every view animates the same move. Colors follow identity: each tree node shares its color with its triangle, its tile of the Dyck path, and its arc in the pairing. Below, the Tamari lattice: drag the ring along edges to walk the flip graph (left comb at the bottom, right comb at the top). With “Color lattice edges” on, edges are colored by which two operator slots the rotation re-associates – in Loday's associahedron these are exactly the parallel classes of edges. (These colors are unrelated to the ones above.)

One permutation, several notations, all in sync. Drag tiles in the bottom row of the two-line notation to reorder; switch to *adjacent only* and each step literally appends a generator to the word (the inversion count ticks; the word is reduced exactly when its length equals the inversion count). Drag a node in the cycle diagram into any cycle at any position. Drag a dot in the matrix within its column. Drag a crossing in the wiring diagram past its neighbor to commute them. In a braid sᵢsⱼsᵢ, drag the middle crossing vertically, or drag the strand that bends around it across it, to get sⱼsᵢsⱼ. Either way the word changes, π doesn't. Drag a straight bit of strand over its neighbor to write sᵢsᵢ; drag the apex of such a double crossing back to cancel it. The permutohedron (n ≤ 4) maps every permutation to a vertex, with edges for adjacent transpositions; drag the token along edges to walk (and write) a word. Push the walk across a face to rewrite the word the same ways: drag a corner across a square to commute, or the middle of three edges around a hexagon across it to braid; where the walk goes out along an edge and straight back, push the tip back to cancel the sᵢsᵢ. For n = 4 the permutohedron is a truncated octahedron: drag a face to turn it.

One braid, as a diagram and as a word in the generators σᵢ, with its strands seen end-on alongside. Every drag on the diagram is a relation of the braid group, so the braid never changes; only its word does. Drag a crossing past a far-away neighbor to commute them. In a braid σᵢσⱼσᵢ (strands layered consistently), drag the middle crossing vertically, or drag the bypassing strand across it. Drag a straight bit of strand across its neighbor to pass in front of it and back (the strand you drag passes in front); drag the apex of such a pair back to cancel it. The apex of a *full twist* σᵢσᵢ won't budge: that is not the identity here. Hover over the diagram to see the strands as points moving in a plane, each crossing a half-turn of two points around each other. Add crossings at the end by turning a point around its neighbor, in front or behind.

Close the braid up to see it as a link. Every drag on the diagram is then a Markov move or a relation, so the link never changes; only its braid does. Strands are colored by the component of the link they belong to. Drag the last crossing on around its loops and in at the front to conjugate (or the first one back around). Pull the bottom strand down at either end of the braid to stabilize, adding a strand, a loop, and a crossing at that end of the word, where the strand you pull passes in front. When the bottom strand crosses only once, at either end, pull the innermost loop back in to destabilize.

A [plane partition](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plane_partition>) is a stack of cubes in the corner of a box – and, seen flat, it is a lozenge tiling of a hexagon. Drag a corner cube to move it or to toss it in the spare pile; drag a spare cube into any inner corner. Each move is one "flip" of the tiling. See also [aztec-diamond](<#/demos/aztec-diamond>), the domino cousin of this demo.

Domino tilings of the [Aztec diamond](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_diamond>). Two parallel dominoes side by side form a 2×2 block; drag one of them to turn the block like a knob, either way and as far round as you like; let go and it settles to the nearest quarter turn. The numbers are Thurston's height function – each flip changes it at exactly one vertex. See also [plane-partition](<#/demos/plane-partition>), the lozenge cousin of this demo.

Drag any non-root node **upward**. Each splay step (zig, zig-zig, zig-zag) is a `d.between` from the current tree to the tree one step later, with a chained snap radius, so a single drag to the root plays out as a sequence of rotations. Nodes are laid out by in-order rank, so rotations only move nodes vertically.
notes.title: Splay tree

A knot diagram you can manipulate by [Reidemeister moves](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reidemeister_move>). Each strand between two crossings is a single curve. Grab one by its middle: drag it onto a ring beside it to twist a loop (R1), push it across a neighboring strand (R2; hold `Alt` to pass under), or slide it across a crossing (R3; or drag the crossing across the strand). Drag a loop back into the strand or a bigon back across its partner to undo. Drag in other directions to bend the strand, or drag a crossing to move it. The Jones polynomial never changes; crossing number and writhe do. Tangle A is the [Culprit](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_unknot>), an unknot that can't be simplified until you first make it worse. Tangle B is a trefoil in disguise.

A **stock-and-flow** editor. Stocks (boxes) accumulate; flows (pipes) fill and drain them, from and to clouds outside the model or between stocks; dashed links say what a flow’s rate depends on. A rate is its constant times one factor per link, and each link’s chip says which shape that factor has (click it to cycle: linear, threshold, gap, saturating, crowding, repression).

Drag a stock’s side arrows to pull out a flow, its top dot to pull out a link onto a valve; drag a flow’s ends onto stocks or off into clouds; drag things to the trash to delete them. Drag sliders, the starting points of the curves, and the time cursor. Click a parameter’s name to see how the long-run behavior depends on it. Double-click names and values to edit them.
